# P1: Local densities and summable spectral coefficients

Let μ be the Möbius function, φ Euler's totient, ζ the Riemann zeta function, and c=ζ(2)^(−1). All products below are over primes. For every integer q≥1 and integer l, the density g(q,l) from problem.md equals q^(−1)Σ_{m≥1, gcd(m²,q)|l} μ(m)gcd(m²,q)/m². Equivalently, it is zero if some p² divides both q and l; otherwise it equals (c/q)∏_{p|q}(1−p^(−2))^(−1)∏_{p||q, p|l}(1−p^(−1)). In particular 0≤g(q,l)≤1/q. Define the multiplicative function G by G(1)=1, G(p)=G(p²)=−1/(p²−1), and G(p^a)=0 for a≥3. Put γ(r)=cG(r), λ(r)=φ(r)γ(r)², and c_r(n)=Σ_{1≤a≤r, gcd(a,r)=1} exp(2πian/r). Then qΣ_{l=1}^q g(q,l)²=Σ_{r|q}λ(r), Σ_{r≥1}λ(r)=c, and, for every integer n≥1, the absolutely convergent series Σ_{r≥1}γ(r)²c_r(n) equals 𝔖(n)=∏_p(1−2/p²)∏_{p²|n}(p²−1)/(p²−2). There is an absolute constant C such that, uniformly for real R≥2, Σ_{r>R}λ(r)≤CR^(−1/2)(log(2R))² and Σ_{r≤R}rλ(r)≤CR^(1/2)(log(2R))².
# Proof of P1

Write \(e(t)=\exp(2\pi i t)\), and take logarithms to base \(e\). All sums over integers below are over positive integers unless another range is specified. We prove the assertions directly; no external literature or dependency proposition is used.

## Existence and evaluation of the density

For every positive integer \(n\), prime factorization gives
\[
\sum_{m^2\mid n}\mu(m)
=\prod_{p^2\mid n}(1-1)=\mu^2(n),
\tag{1}
\]
where an empty product equals one. Fix \(q\geq1\) and \(l\in\mathbb Z\). For \(x\geq1\), put \(M=\lfloor\sqrt{x}\rfloor\) and \(d_m=(m^2,q)\). The simultaneous congruences
\[
n\equiv l\pmod q,\qquad n\equiv0\pmod{m^2}
\]
are soluble precisely when \(d_m\mid l\). Indeed, writing \(n=m^2k\) reduces them to a linear congruence in \(k\); division by \(d_m\) leaves a coefficient coprime to \(q/d_m\). When soluble, the solutions form one residue class modulo \(qm^2/d_m\). The number of its members in \([1,x]\) differs from \(xd_m/(qm^2)\) by at most one. Consequently (1) gives
\[
Q(x;q,l)=\frac{x}{q}
\sum_{\substack{m\leq M\\d_m\mid l}}
\frac{\mu(m)d_m}{m^2}+E_1,
\qquad |E_1|\leq M.
\tag{2}
\]
Here each counting error has absolute value at most one, and there are at most \(M\) terms, so their sum has absolute value at most \(M\).

The series
\[
D(q,l)=\frac1q\sum_{\substack{m\geq1\\d_m\mid l}}
\frac{\mu(m)d_m}{m^2}
\tag{3}
\]
converges absolutely: each summand has absolute value at most \(m^{-2}\), since \(d_m\leq q\). The infinite omitted tail in (2), after multiplication by \(x\), has absolute value at most
\[
x\sum_{m>M}\frac1{m^2}
\leq x\int_M^\infty t^{-2}\,dt=\frac{x}{M}.
\tag{4}
\]
Since \(\sqrt{x}/2\leq M\leq\sqrt{x}\), equations (2)--(4) prove the explicit estimate
\[
|Q(x;q,l)-xD(q,l)|
\leq M+\frac{x}{M}\leq3\sqrt{x},
\qquad x\geq1.
\tag{5}
\]
Dividing by \(x\) and letting \(x\) tend to infinity proves that the density from `problem.md` exists and equals (3).

We will use the elementary Euler identity
\[
c=\zeta(2)^{-1}=\prod_p(1-p^{-2}).
\tag{6}
\]
To justify it here, expanding \(\prod_{p\leq z}(1-p^{-2})^{-1}\) gives the sum of \(m^{-2}\) over integers all of whose prime factors are at most \(z\). These sums increase to \(\sum_{m\geq1}m^{-2}=\zeta(2)\), because every integer has finitely many prime factors. Taking reciprocals gives (6).

For a prime \(p\), let \(t=v_p(q)\). The summand in (3) vanishes unless \(m\) is squarefree. The choice to include \(p\) in such an \(m\) contributes
\(-p^{\min(2,t)-2}\), and is allowed precisely when
\(p^{\min(2,t)}\mid l\). Thus the local factor in \(qg(q,l)\) is
\[
\begin{cases}
1-p^{-2},&t=0,\\
1,&t=1,\ p\nmid l,\\
1-p^{-1},&t=1,\ p\mid l,\\
1,&t\geq2,\ p^2\nmid l,\\
0,&t\geq2,\ p^2\mid l.
\end{cases}
\tag{7}
\]
This Euler expansion is justified by the absolute convergence of (3); equivalently, expand over finitely many primes and pass to the absolutely convergent series. The divisibility conditions in (7) also apply to \(l=0\).

If some \(p^2\) divides both \(q\) and \(l\), (7) gives \(g(q,l)=0\). In every other case, combining (6) and (7) gives exactly
\[
g(q,l)=\frac cq
\prod_{p\mid q}(1-p^{-2})^{-1}
\prod_{\substack{p\parallel q\\p\mid l}}(1-p^{-1}).
\tag{8}
\]
Every local factor in (7) lies in \([0,1]\). Their product therefore lies in \([0,1]\), proving
\[
0\leq g(q,l)\leq\frac1q.
\tag{9}
\]

## The finite second-moment identity

Let
\[
L(r)=\varphi(r)G(r)^2,
\qquad \lambda(r)=c^2L(r).
\]
The function \(L\) is multiplicative. Its prime-power values are
\[
L(p)=\frac{p-1}{(p^2-1)^2},\qquad
L(p^2)=\frac{p(p-1)}{(p^2-1)^2},\qquad
L(p^j)=0\quad(j\geq3).
\tag{10}
\]
These formulas follow from counting the \(p^j-p^{j-1}\) residues coprime to \(p^j\); multiplicativity of \(\varphi\) follows from the Chinese remainder theorem.

For \(t\geq1\), define a function on residues modulo \(p^t\) by
\[
b_{p,t}(l)=
\begin{cases}
1-p^{-1},&t=1,\ p\mid l,\\
0,&t\geq2,\ p^2\mid l,\\
1,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
Equations (7)--(8), including their zero cases, give
\[
qg(q,l)=c\prod_{p^t\parallel q}
(1-p^{-2})^{-1}b_{p,t}(l).
\tag{11}
\]
For \(t=1\), there are \(p-1\) residues with \(b_{p,1}=1\) and one with \(b_{p,1}=1-p^{-1}\). Hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
(1-p^{-2})^{-2}\frac1p\sum_{l\bmod p}b_{p,1}(l)^2
&=(1-p^{-2})^{-2}
\left(1-\frac2{p^2}+\frac1{p^3}\right)\\
&=\frac{p^4-2p^2+p}{(p^2-1)^2}\\
&=1+\frac{p-1}{(p^2-1)^2}=1+L(p).
\end{aligned}
\tag{12}
\]
For \(t\geq2\), precisely \(p^{t-2}\) of the \(p^t\) residues have \(b_{p,t}=0\), and the other \(p^t-p^{t-2}\) have value one. Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
(1-p^{-2})^{-2}\frac1{p^t}
\sum_{l\bmod p^t}b_{p,t}(l)^2
&=(1-p^{-2})^{-1}\\
&=1+\frac1{p^2-1}\\
&=1+L(p)+L(p^2).
\end{aligned}
\tag{13}
\]
The last equality uses
\((p-1)+p(p-1)=p^2-1\).

The Chinese remainder theorem identifies the \(q\) residues modulo \(q\) with the Cartesian product of the residue sets modulo its prime-power factors. Averaging the square of (11) consequently factors into the local averages (12)--(13). With empty products understood when \(q=1\), this yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
q\sum_{l=1}^qg(q,l)^2
&=\frac1q\sum_{l=1}^q(qg(q,l))^2\\
&=c^2\prod_{p^t\parallel q}
\left(1+\sum_{j=1}^tL(p^j)\right)\\
&=c^2\sum_{r\mid q}L(r)
=\sum_{r\mid q}\lambda(r).
\end{aligned}
\tag{14}
\]

## Absolute summability and explicit tail estimates

The support of \(L\) consists of integers with no prime exponent exceeding two. Every such integer has a unique representation
\[
r=ab^2,
\qquad a,b\text{ squarefree},\quad(a,b)=1.
\tag{15}
\]
For every prime \(p\geq2\), set
\[
A_p=\frac{p^3}{(p-1)(p+1)^2}.
\]
The denominator minus the numerator equals \(p^2-p-1\), which is at least one for \(p\geq2\). Thus \(0<A_p\leq1\), and (10) becomes
\[
L(p)=\frac{A_p}{p^3},\qquad
L(p^2)=\frac{A_p}{p^2}.
\]
Multiplying these inequalities over the prime factors in (15) proves
\[
0\leq\lambda(ab^2)\leq\frac{c^2}{a^3b^2}.
\tag{16}
\]
Dropping the restrictions on \(a,b\) only increases these nonnegative sums. In particular
\[
\sum_{r\geq1}\lambda(r)
\leq c^2\left(\sum_{a\geq1}a^{-3}\right)
\left(\sum_{b\geq1}b^{-2}\right)
\leq3c^2<\infty,
\tag{17}
\]
where the two series are bounded by
\(1+\int_1^\infty t^{-3}dt=3/2\) and
\(1+\int_1^\infty t^{-2}dt=2\), respectively.

We can now evaluate the sum by its absolutely convergent Euler product. Equation (10) gives
\[
1+L(p)+L(p^2)
=1+\frac1{p^2-1}=(1-p^{-2})^{-1}.
\]
Consequently (6) implies
\[
\sum_{r\geq1}\lambda(r)
=c^2\prod_p(1+L(p)+L(p^2))
=c^2\zeta(2)=c.
\tag{18}
\]

For every real \(T>0\), we have the explicit bound
\[
\sum_{b>T}\frac1{b^2}\leq\frac2T.
\tag{19}
\]
For \(T\geq1\), putting \(N=\lfloor T\rfloor\geq T/2\) bounds this infinite tail by
\(\int_N^\infty t^{-2}dt=1/N\leq2/T\).
For \(0<T<1\), the sum is at most \(2\), which is at most \(2/T\).
For any \(R>0\), (16) and then (19), with \(T=\sqrt{R/a}\), give
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{r>R}\lambda(r)
&\leq c^2\sum_{a\geq1}\frac1{a^3}
\sum_{b>\sqrt{R/a}}\frac1{b^2}\\
&\leq2c^2R^{-1/2}\sum_{a\geq1}a^{-5/2}\\
&\leq\frac{10}{3}R^{-1/2}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{20}
\]
For each \(a\), the inner infinite sum before summation over \(a\) is at most \(2\sqrt{a/R}\). Its contribution after multiplication by \(c^2a^{-3}\) is at most \(2c^2R^{-1/2}a^{-5/2}\). The final bound uses \(c\leq1\) and
\[
\sum_{a\geq1}a^{-5/2}
\leq1+\int_1^\infty t^{-5/2}dt=\frac53.
\tag{21}
\]

Multiplication of (16) by \(ab^2\) gives
\(ab^2\lambda(ab^2)\leq c^2a^{-2}\). Thus
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{r\leq R}r\lambda(r)
&\leq c^2\sum_{1\leq a\leq R}\frac1{a^2}
\sum_{1\leq b\leq\sqrt{R/a}}1\\
&\leq c^2R^{1/2}\sum_{1\leq a\leq R}a^{-5/2}
\leq\frac53R^{1/2}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{22}
\]
For each \(a\leq R\), the inner sum has
\(\lfloor\sqrt{R/a}\rfloor\leq\sqrt{R/a}\) terms, each contributing at most \(c^2a^{-2}\). Its total is at most \(c^2R^{1/2}a^{-5/2}\). Summing over the \(\lfloor R\rfloor\) possible values of \(a\), and applying (21), gives the last inequality in (22).

For \(R\geq2\), \(\log(2R)\geq\log4>1\). Therefore (20) and (22) imply both bounds requested in the statement, with the same absolute constant \(C=10/3\). They also prove the stronger versions without logarithmic factors.

## The Ramanujan series

There are \(\varphi(r)\) terms in the defining sum for \(c_r(n)\), each of absolute value one. Hence, for every integer \(n\),
\[
|c_r(n)|\leq\varphi(r),\qquad
\sum_{r\geq1}|\gamma(r)^2c_r(n)|
\leq\sum_{r\geq1}\lambda(r)=c.
\tag{23}
\]
This proves absolute convergence, with a bound uniform in \(n\).

For completeness, the multiplicativity needed to evaluate the series follows directly from the Chinese remainder theorem. If \((s,t)=1\), choose integers \(u,v\) with \(tu\equiv1\pmod s\) and \(sv\equiv1\pmod t\). A unit residue \(a\pmod{st}\) corresponding to unit residues \(b\pmod s\), \(d\pmod t\) satisfies
\[
\frac{a}{st}\equiv\frac{bu}{s}+\frac{dv}{t}\pmod1.
\]
Summing the resulting exponential identity over \(b,d\), and using the permutations of unit residues induced by multiplication by \(u,v\), gives
\[
c_{st}(n)=c_s(n)c_t(n).
\tag{24}
\]

The finite geometric sum satisfies
\[
\sum_{a=1}^k e(an/k)=k\,\boldsymbol1_{k\mid n}.
\]
Subtracting the term for the zero residue modulo \(p\) gives
\(c_p(n)=p\boldsymbol1_{p\mid n}-1\).
Subtracting the sum over residues divisible by \(p\) from the full sum modulo \(p^2\) gives
\[
c_{p^2}(n)=p^2\boldsymbol1_{p^2\mid n}
-p\boldsymbol1_{p\mid n}.
\]
Adding these two exact identities yields
\[
c_p(n)+c_{p^2}(n)=p^2\boldsymbol1_{p^2\mid n}-1.
\tag{25}
\]
By (23)--(24), the absolutely convergent series has the Euler expansion
\[
\sum_{r\geq1}\gamma(r)^2c_r(n)
=c^2\prod_p
\left(1+\frac{c_p(n)+c_{p^2}(n)}{(p^2-1)^2}\right).
\tag{26}
\]
Using (6), absorb the factor \((1-p^{-2})^2\) of \(c^2\) into each local factor. If \(p^2\nmid n\), (25) gives
\[
(1-p^{-2})^2\left(1-\frac1{(p^2-1)^2}\right)
=\frac{(p^2-1)^2-1}{p^4}
=1-\frac2{p^2}.
\tag{27}
\]
If \(p^2\mid n\), it gives
\[
(1-p^{-2})^2\left(1+\frac{p^2-1}{(p^2-1)^2}\right)
=\frac{p^2-1}{p^2}
=1-\frac1{p^2}.
\tag{28}
\]
All these product operations are legitimate: (26) is justified by absolute convergence, and (6) converges. The product \(\prod_p(1-2/p^2)\) converges to a positive number as well. Indeed, for \(0\leq u\leq1/2\),
\(-\log(1-u)=\int_0^u(1-t)^{-1}dt\leq2u\), so
\(\sum_p|\log(1-2/p^2)|\leq4\sum_p p^{-2}<\infty\).

Finally, when \(n\geq1\), only finitely many primes satisfy \(p^2\mid n\). Replacing the factors (27) by (28) for those primes multiplies the baseline product by
\[
\frac{1-p^{-2}}{1-2p^{-2}}=\frac{p^2-1}{p^2-2}.
\]
Thus (26) equals precisely
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
\mathfrak S(n)=\prod_p\left(1-\frac2{p^2}\right)
\prod_{p^2\mid n}\frac{p^2-1}{p^2-2}.}
\]
This proves every assertion of P1.

No numerical checks or external sources were used.

     1	# Proof of P1
     2	
     3	Write \(e(t)=\exp(2\pi i t)\), and take logarithms to base \(e\). All sums over integers below are over positive integers unless another range is specified. We prove the assertions directly; no external literature or dependency proposition is used.
     4	
     5	## Existence and evaluation of the density
     6	
     7	For every positive integer \(n\), prime factorization gives
     8	\[
     9	\sum_{m^2\mid n}\mu(m)
    10	=\prod_{p^2\mid n}(1-1)=\mu^2(n),
    11	\tag{1}
    12	\]
    13	where an empty product equals one. Fix \(q\geq1\) and \(l\in\mathbb Z\). For \(x\geq1\), put \(M=\lfloor\sqrt{x}\rfloor\) and \(d_m=(m^2,q)\). The simultaneous congruences
    14	\[
    15	n\equiv l\pmod q,\qquad n\equiv0\pmod{m^2}
    16	\]
    17	are soluble precisely when \(d_m\mid l\). Indeed, writing \(n=m^2k\) reduces them to a linear congruence in \(k\); division by \(d_m\) leaves a coefficient coprime to \(q/d_m\). When soluble, the solutions form one residue class modulo \(qm^2/d_m\). The number of its members in \([1,x]\) differs from \(xd_m/(qm^2)\) by at most one. Consequently (1) gives
    18	\[
    19	Q(x;q,l)=\frac{x}{q}
    20	\sum_{\substack{m\leq M\\d_m\mid l}}
    21	\frac{\mu(m)d_m}{m^2}+E_1,
    22	\qquad |E_1|\leq M.
    23	\tag{2}
    24	\]
    25	Here each counting error has absolute value at most one, and there are at most \(M\) terms, so their sum has absolute value at most \(M\).
    26	
    27	The series
    28	\[
    29	D(q,l)=\frac1q\sum_{\substack{m\geq1\\d_m\mid l}}
    30	\frac{\mu(m)d_m}{m^2}
    31	\tag{3}
    32	\]
    33	converges absolutely: each summand has absolute value at most \(m^{-2}\), since \(d_m\leq q\). The infinite omitted tail in (2), after multiplication by \(x\), has absolute value at most
    34	\[
    35	x\sum_{m>M}\frac1{m^2}
    36	\leq x\int_M^\infty t^{-2}\,dt=\frac{x}{M}.
    37	\tag{4}
    38	\]
    39	Since \(\sqrt{x}/2\leq M\leq\sqrt{x}\), equations (2)--(4) prove the explicit estimate
    40	\[
    41	|Q(x;q,l)-xD(q,l)|
    42	\leq M+\frac{x}{M}\leq3\sqrt{x},
    43	\qquad x\geq1.
    44	\tag{5}
    45	\]
    46	Dividing by \(x\) and letting \(x\) tend to infinity proves that the density from `problem.md` exists and equals (3).
    47	
    48	We will use the elementary Euler identity
    49	\[
    50	c=\zeta(2)^{-1}=\prod_p(1-p^{-2}).
    51	\tag{6}
    52	\]
    53	To justify it here, expanding \(\prod_{p\leq z}(1-p^{-2})^{-1}\) gives the sum of \(m^{-2}\) over integers all of whose prime factors are at most \(z\). These sums increase to \(\sum_{m\geq1}m^{-2}=\zeta(2)\), because every integer has finitely many prime factors. Taking reciprocals gives (6).
    54	
    55	For a prime \(p\), let \(t=v_p(q)\). The summand in (3) vanishes unless \(m\) is squarefree. The choice to include \(p\) in such an \(m\) contributes
    56	\(-p^{\min(2,t)-2}\), and is allowed precisely when
    57	\(p^{\min(2,t)}\mid l\). Thus the local factor in \(qg(q,l)\) is
    58	\[
    59	\begin{cases}
    60	1-p^{-2},&t=0,\\
    61	1,&t=1,\ p\nmid l,\\
    62	1-p^{-1},&t=1,\ p\mid l,\\
    63	1,&t\geq2,\ p^2\nmid l,\\
    64	0,&t\geq2,\ p^2\mid l.
    65	\end{cases}
    66	\tag{7}
    67	\]
    68	This Euler expansion is justified by the absolute convergence of (3); equivalently, expand over finitely many primes and pass to the absolutely convergent series. The divisibility conditions in (7) also apply to \(l=0\).
    69	
    70	If some \(p^2\) divides both \(q\) and \(l\), (7) gives \(g(q,l)=0\). In every other case, combining (6) and (7) gives exactly
    71	\[
    72	g(q,l)=\frac cq
    73	\prod_{p\mid q}(1-p^{-2})^{-1}
    74	\prod_{\substack{p\parallel q\\p\mid l}}(1-p^{-1}).
    75	\tag{8}
    76	\]
    77	Every local factor in (7) lies in \([0,1]\). Their product therefore lies in \([0,1]\), proving
    78	\[
    79	0\leq g(q,l)\leq\frac1q.
    80	\tag{9}
    81	\]
    82	
    83	## The finite second-moment identity
    84	
    85	Let
    86	\[
    87	L(r)=\varphi(r)G(r)^2,
    88	\qquad \lambda(r)=c^2L(r).
    89	\]
    90	The function \(L\) is multiplicative. Its prime-power values are
    91	\[
    92	L(p)=\frac{p-1}{(p^2-1)^2},\qquad
    93	L(p^2)=\frac{p(p-1)}{(p^2-1)^2},\qquad
    94	L(p^j)=0\quad(j\geq3).
    95	\tag{10}
    96	\]
    97	These formulas follow from counting the \(p^j-p^{j-1}\) residues coprime to \(p^j\); multiplicativity of \(\varphi\) follows from the Chinese remainder theorem.
    98	
    99	For \(t\geq1\), define a function on residues modulo \(p^t\) by
   100	\[
   101	b_{p,t}(l)=
   102	\begin{cases}
   103	1-p^{-1},&t=1,\ p\mid l,\\
   104	0,&t\geq2,\ p^2\mid l,\\
   105	1,&\text{otherwise}.
   106	\end{cases}
   107	\]
   108	Equations (7)--(8), including their zero cases, give
   109	\[
   110	qg(q,l)=c\prod_{p^t\parallel q}
   111	(1-p^{-2})^{-1}b_{p,t}(l).
   112	\tag{11}
   113	\]
   114	For \(t=1\), there are \(p-1\) residues with \(b_{p,1}=1\) and one with \(b_{p,1}=1-p^{-1}\). Hence
   115	\[
   116	\begin{aligned}
   117	(1-p^{-2})^{-2}\frac1p\sum_{l\bmod p}b_{p,1}(l)^2
   118	&=(1-p^{-2})^{-2}
   119	\left(1-\frac2{p^2}+\frac1{p^3}\right)\\
   120	&=\frac{p^4-2p^2+p}{(p^2-1)^2}\\
   121	&=1+\frac{p-1}{(p^2-1)^2}=1+L(p).
   122	\end{aligned}
   123	\tag{12}
   124	\]
   125	For \(t\geq2\), precisely \(p^{t-2}\) of the \(p^t\) residues have \(b_{p,t}=0\), and the other \(p^t-p^{t-2}\) have value one. Therefore
   126	\[
   127	\begin{aligned}
   128	(1-p^{-2})^{-2}\frac1{p^t}
   129	\sum_{l\bmod p^t}b_{p,t}(l)^2
   130	&=(1-p^{-2})^{-1}\\
   131	&=1+\frac1{p^2-1}\\
   132	&=1+L(p)+L(p^2).
   133	\end{aligned}
   134	\tag{13}
   135	\]
   136	The last equality uses
   137	\((p-1)+p(p-1)=p^2-1\).
   138	
   139	The Chinese remainder theorem identifies the \(q\) residues modulo \(q\) with the Cartesian product of the residue sets modulo its prime-power factors. Averaging the square of (11) consequently factors into the local averages (12)--(13). With empty products understood when \(q=1\), this yields
   140	\[
   141	\begin{aligned}
   142	q\sum_{l=1}^qg(q,l)^2
   143	&=\frac1q\sum_{l=1}^q(qg(q,l))^2\\
   144	&=c^2\prod_{p^t\parallel q}
   145	\left(1+\sum_{j=1}^tL(p^j)\right)\\
   146	&=c^2\sum_{r\mid q}L(r)
   147	=\sum_{r\mid q}\lambda(r).
   148	\end{aligned}
   149	\tag{14}
   150	\]
   151	
   152	## Absolute summability and explicit tail estimates
   153	
   154	The support of \(L\) consists of integers with no prime exponent exceeding two. Every such integer has a unique representation
   155	\[
   156	r=ab^2,
   157	\qquad a,b\text{ squarefree},\quad(a,b)=1.
   158	\tag{15}
   159	\]
   160	For every prime \(p\geq2\), set
   161	\[
   162	A_p=\frac{p^3}{(p-1)(p+1)^2}.
   163	\]
   164	The denominator minus the numerator equals \(p^2-p-1\), which is at least one for \(p\geq2\). Thus \(0<A_p\leq1\), and (10) becomes
   165	\[
   166	L(p)=\frac{A_p}{p^3},\qquad
   167	L(p^2)=\frac{A_p}{p^2}.
   168	\]
   169	Multiplying these inequalities over the prime factors in (15) proves
   170	\[
   171	0\leq\lambda(ab^2)\leq\frac{c^2}{a^3b^2}.
   172	\tag{16}
   173	\]
   174	Dropping the restrictions on \(a,b\) only increases these nonnegative sums. In particular
   175	\[
   176	\sum_{r\geq1}\lambda(r)
   177	\leq c^2\left(\sum_{a\geq1}a^{-3}\right)
   178	\left(\sum_{b\geq1}b^{-2}\right)
   179	\leq3c^2<\infty,
   180	\tag{17}
   181	\]
   182	where the two series are bounded by
   183	\(1+\int_1^\infty t^{-3}dt=3/2\) and
   184	\(1+\int_1^\infty t^{-2}dt=2\), respectively.
   185	
   186	We can now evaluate the sum by its absolutely convergent Euler product. Equation (10) gives
   187	\[
   188	1+L(p)+L(p^2)
   189	=1+\frac1{p^2-1}=(1-p^{-2})^{-1}.
   190	\]
   191	Consequently (6) implies
   192	\[
   193	\sum_{r\geq1}\lambda(r)
   194	=c^2\prod_p(1+L(p)+L(p^2))
   195	=c^2\zeta(2)=c.
   196	\tag{18}
   197	\]
   198	
   199	For every real \(T>0\), we have the explicit bound
   200	\[
   201	\sum_{b>T}\frac1{b^2}\leq\frac2T.
   202	\tag{19}
   203	\]
   204	For \(T\geq1\), putting \(N=\lfloor T\rfloor\geq T/2\) bounds this infinite tail by
   205	\(\int_N^\infty t^{-2}dt=1/N\leq2/T\).
   206	For \(0<T<1\), the sum is at most \(2\), which is at most \(2/T\).
   207	For any \(R>0\), (16) and then (19), with \(T=\sqrt{R/a}\), give
   208	\[
   209	\begin{aligned}
   210	\sum_{r>R}\lambda(r)
   211	&\leq c^2\sum_{a\geq1}\frac1{a^3}
   212	\sum_{b>\sqrt{R/a}}\frac1{b^2}\\
   213	&\leq2c^2R^{-1/2}\sum_{a\geq1}a^{-5/2}\\
   214	&\leq\frac{10}{3}R^{-1/2}.
   215	\end{aligned}
   216	\tag{20}
   217	\]
   218	For each \(a\), the inner infinite sum before summation over \(a\) is at most \(2\sqrt{a/R}\). Its contribution after multiplication by \(c^2a^{-3}\) is at most \(2c^2R^{-1/2}a^{-5/2}\). The final bound uses \(c\leq1\) and
   219	\[
   220	\sum_{a\geq1}a^{-5/2}
   221	\leq1+\int_1^\infty t^{-5/2}dt=\frac53.
   222	\tag{21}
   223	\]
   224	
   225	Multiplication of (16) by \(ab^2\) gives
   226	\(ab^2\lambda(ab^2)\leq c^2a^{-2}\). Thus
   227	\[
   228	\begin{aligned}
   229	\sum_{r\leq R}r\lambda(r)
   230	&\leq c^2\sum_{1\leq a\leq R}\frac1{a^2}
   231	\sum_{1\leq b\leq\sqrt{R/a}}1\\
   232	&\leq c^2R^{1/2}\sum_{1\leq a\leq R}a^{-5/2}
   233	\leq\frac53R^{1/2}.
   234	\end{aligned}
   235	\tag{22}
   236	\]
   237	For each \(a\leq R\), the inner sum has
   238	\(\lfloor\sqrt{R/a}\rfloor\leq\sqrt{R/a}\) terms, each contributing at most \(c^2a^{-2}\). Its total is at most \(c^2R^{1/2}a^{-5/2}\). Summing over the \(\lfloor R\rfloor\) possible values of \(a\), and applying (21), gives the last inequality in (22).
   239	
   240	For \(R\geq2\), \(\log(2R)\geq\log4>1\). Therefore (20) and (22) imply both bounds requested in the statement, with the same absolute constant \(C=10/3\). They also prove the stronger versions without logarithmic factors.
   241	
   242	## The Ramanujan series
   243	
   244	There are \(\varphi(r)\) terms in the defining sum for \(c_r(n)\), each of absolute value one. Hence, for every integer \(n\),
   245	\[
   246	|c_r(n)|\leq\varphi(r),\qquad
   247	\sum_{r\geq1}|\gamma(r)^2c_r(n)|
   248	\leq\sum_{r\geq1}\lambda(r)=c.
   249	\tag{23}
   250	\]
   251	This proves absolute convergence, with a bound uniform in \(n\).
   252	
   253	For completeness, the multiplicativity needed to evaluate the series follows directly from the Chinese remainder theorem. If \((s,t)=1\), choose integers \(u,v\) with \(tu\equiv1\pmod s\) and \(sv\equiv1\pmod t\). A unit residue \(a\pmod{st}\) corresponding to unit residues \(b\pmod s\), \(d\pmod t\) satisfies
   254	\[
   255	\frac{a}{st}\equiv\frac{bu}{s}+\frac{dv}{t}\pmod1.
   256	\]
   257	Summing the resulting exponential identity over \(b,d\), and using the permutations of unit residues induced by multiplication by \(u,v\), gives
   258	\[
   259	c_{st}(n)=c_s(n)c_t(n).
   260	\tag{24}
   261	\]
   262	
   263	The finite geometric sum satisfies
   264	\[
   265	\sum_{a=1}^k e(an/k)=k\,\boldsymbol1_{k\mid n}.
   266	\]
   267	Subtracting the term for the zero residue modulo \(p\) gives
   268	\(c_p(n)=p\boldsymbol1_{p\mid n}-1\).
   269	Subtracting the sum over residues divisible by \(p\) from the full sum modulo \(p^2\) gives
   270	\[
   271	c_{p^2}(n)=p^2\boldsymbol1_{p^2\mid n}
   272	-p\boldsymbol1_{p\mid n}.
   273	\]
   274	Adding these two exact identities yields
   275	\[
   276	c_p(n)+c_{p^2}(n)=p^2\boldsymbol1_{p^2\mid n}-1.
   277	\tag{25}
   278	\]
   279	By (23)--(24), the absolutely convergent series has the Euler expansion
   280	\[
   281	\sum_{r\geq1}\gamma(r)^2c_r(n)
   282	=c^2\prod_p
   283	\left(1+\frac{c_p(n)+c_{p^2}(n)}{(p^2-1)^2}\right).
   284	\tag{26}
   285	\]
   286	Using (6), absorb the factor \((1-p^{-2})^2\) of \(c^2\) into each local factor. If \(p^2\nmid n\), (25) gives
   287	\[
   288	(1-p^{-2})^2\left(1-\frac1{(p^2-1)^2}\right)
   289	=\frac{(p^2-1)^2-1}{p^4}
   290	=1-\frac2{p^2}.
   291	\tag{27}
   292	\]
   293	If \(p^2\mid n\), it gives
   294	\[
   295	(1-p^{-2})^2\left(1+\frac{p^2-1}{(p^2-1)^2}\right)
   296	=\frac{p^2-1}{p^2}
   297	=1-\frac1{p^2}.
   298	\tag{28}
   299	\]
   300	All these product operations are legitimate: (26) is justified by absolute convergence, and (6) converges. The product \(\prod_p(1-2/p^2)\) converges to a positive number as well. Indeed, for \(0\leq u\leq1/2\),
   301	\(-\log(1-u)=\int_0^u(1-t)^{-1}dt\leq2u\), so
   302	\(\sum_p|\log(1-2/p^2)|\leq4\sum_p p^{-2}<\infty\).
   303	
   304	Finally, when \(n\geq1\), only finitely many primes satisfy \(p^2\mid n\). Replacing the factors (27) by (28) for those primes multiplies the baseline product by
   305	\[
   306	\frac{1-p^{-2}}{1-2p^{-2}}=\frac{p^2-1}{p^2-2}.
   307	\]
   308	Thus (26) equals precisely
   309	\[
   310	\boxed{\displaystyle
   311	\mathfrak S(n)=\prod_p\left(1-\frac2{p^2}\right)
   312	\prod_{p^2\mid n}\frac{p^2-1}{p^2-2}.}
   313	\]
   314	This proves every assertion of P1.

# Problem: squarefree numbers in arithmetic progressions to polynomial moduli

## Notation

- $\mu^2(n)$ is the indicator of squarefree $n$.
- $Q(x;q,l) = \#\{n \le x : n \equiv l \pmod q,\ n \text{ squarefree}\}$.
- $g(q,l) = \lim_{x\to\infty} Q(x;q,l)/x$ (exists; derive its closed form yourself if you need it).
- $E(x;q,l) = Q(x;q,l) - g(q,l)\,x$.
- $f \in \mathbb{Z}[t]$ is a polynomial of degree $d \ge 1$ with $f(t) \ge 2$ and $f'(t) \ge 1$ for $t \ge 1$.
- $\rho(m) = \#\{a \bmod m : f(a) \equiv 0 \pmod m\}$.

## Object of study

$$
V_f(x,y) = \sum_{k \le y} f'(k) \sum_{l=1}^{f(k)} E(x; f(k), l)^2 ,
\qquad f(y) \le x .
$$

The weight $f'(k)$ makes the sparse sum over moduli comparable to the full
Montgomery–Hooley variance $V(x,Y) = \sum_{q\le Y}\sum_{l\le q} E(x;q,l)^2$ with
$Y = f(y)$.

## Question

Determine the asymptotic behaviour of $V_f(x,y)$: a main term with an explicit
constant depending on $f$, and error terms, in as large a range of
$f(y) \le x$ as you can justify.

A weaker range or a weaker error term is acceptable **if it is correct**.
You may change the weight $f'(k)$ or restrict the class of $f$ if you state the
change explicitly and justify it.

## Context

The `papers/` folder contains:

- R. C. Vaughan (2005), *A variance for k-free numbers in arithmetic
  progressions*, Proc. London Math. Soc. (3) 91, 573–597: the asymptotic for
  the full variance $V(x,Y)$ over all moduli $q \le Y$.
- Brüdern–Wooley (2011), *Sparse variance for primes in arithmetic progression*:
  the analogue of this problem for primes, with moduli $f(k)$.
- Brüdern–Granville–Perelli–Vaughan–Wooley (1998), *On the exponential sum over
  k-free numbers*: major-arc estimates for the exponential sum over squarefree
  numbers.
- Further works listed in `papers/INDEX.md`, if that file exists.

**Literature cutoff.** Besides these papers, use only literature from 2010 or
earlier (see the rules at the end of your instructions).

The expected approach is to adapt Vaughan's method for all moduli to sparse
moduli, as Brüdern–Wooley did for primes. You are not required to follow it.

`numerics/results.json`, once present, holds exact computations of $V_f(x,y)$
for small $x$. It is ground truth: a predicted main term that disagrees with it
is wrong.
